Spot vs perpetual.long:
Spot means buying the asset itself: you pay, you own the coin, and it sits in a wallet or on an exchange. A perpetual is a derivative — a contract whose price tracks the spot price but never expires, settles in a stablecoin or in the coin itself, and involves owning nothing except a position on a venue's ledger.

The tracking is done by the funding rate: periodic peer-to-peer payments between longs and shorts that push the contract price back towards spot. Perps exist mainly to offer leverage. That is their function and their danger — the same move that dents a spot holding by a few percent can erase a leveraged perp position entirely.

Where people get fooled: beginners open a perp believing they bought the coin. They did not — they took a leveraged side bet against everyone else on the venue, complete with funding costs, a liquidation price and exchange counterparty risk. If the plan was to hold for years, spot is the instrument; a perp held for years quietly bleeds funding the whole way.
Spot vs perpetual.usage: Someone says they are holding spot through the volatility — meaning no liquidation price exists on the position, because there is no perp and no leverage involved.

Liquidation cascade.long:
When a leveraged position falls below its maintenance margin, the exchange force-closes it at market. That forced sale pushes price into the liquidation levels of the next tier of leveraged positions, which are then force-closed too. Each round of selling triggers the next: a cascade.

Cascades are why crypto produces violent wicks that seem detached from any news. The fuel is open interest — a stock of leveraged positions clustered at similar entries — and the spark can be almost anything. Once running, the move feeds on the order book rather than on information, and it often snaps back once the forced flow is exhausted.

Where people get fooled: after a cascade, commentators reverse-engineer a fundamental story for what was a mechanical margin event, and traders treat the wick low as the market's considered opinion of value. It is closer to a fire alarm emptying a building — the stampede tells you about the leverage in the room, not about the asset.
Liquidation cascade.usage: A trader describes a two-minute wick through several support levels as a liquidation cascade — forced selling triggering more forced selling, with no news anywhere in sight.

Long squeeze / short squeeze.long:
A squeeze is forced buying or selling by trapped traders. In a short squeeze, rising prices force shorts to buy back, which pushes price higher and forces out more shorts. A long squeeze is the mirror image: falling prices force leveraged longs to sell, accelerating the drop.

The mechanism runs on positioning, not fundamentals. Crowded positioning — visible in funding rates and open interest — is the precondition; the move itself is margin mechanics working through the order book. Squeezes end when the trapped side has been flushed, which is why they so often reverse sharply once the forced flow stops.

Where people get fooled: squeeze moves look like conviction. A short squeeze resembles a bullish breakout backed by genuine demand, so traders chase it — buying from the very shorts who are closing out. When the forced flow dries up there is nothing underneath the price. Telling forced flow from voluntary flow is hard even afterwards; doing it in real time is harder still.
Long squeeze / short squeeze.usage: Funding had gone deeply negative before price ripped through the highs, so the desk read the move as a short squeeze rather than fresh demand.

CEX vs DEX.long:
A centralised exchange (CEX) is a company: it holds your funds, runs an order book on its own servers, and matches trades off-chain. A decentralised exchange (DEX) is a set of smart contracts: you trade from your own wallet, settlement happens on-chain, and the counterparty is usually an automated market maker rather than another order.

The trade-off is custody versus convenience. On a CEX you get speed, depth and fiat ramps, but your coins are an IOU from the company — the FTX collapse in 2022 showed what that IOU is worth when the company fails. On a DEX you keep custody but pay gas, face MEV, and carry smart-contract risk.

Where people get fooled: 'decentralised' gets read as 'safe'. A DEX removes exchange counterparty risk and replaces it with contract bugs, poisoned token listings and your own key management. Neither venue removes risk; each simply chooses which failure modes you are exposed to, and the honest question is which set you are better equipped to survive.
CEX vs DEX.usage: The desk keeps its trading float on a CEX for the depth and moves long-term holdings off into self-custody, treating the two venues as different risk propositions.

Custody.long:
Custody is the question of who actually controls an asset. In crypto that means who holds the private keys. Self-custody means you do; exchange custody means the venue does, and what you own is a claim in their database rather than coins on a chain.

The distinction matters because exchange balances are unsecured IOUs. The FTX collapse in 2022 made this concrete: customer balances turned out to be claims on a bankrupt estate. 'Not your keys, not your coins' is glib but mechanically accurate — an exchange balance is exposed to hacks, freezes, withdrawal halts and insolvency, none of which require you to make a bad trade.

Where people get fooled: self-custody gets treated as the risk-free alternative. It removes counterparty risk and replaces it with operational risk — lost seed phrases, phishing, compromised devices, no recourse and no password reset. Plenty of coins have been lost to each failure mode. The honest framing is choosing which set of risks you are personally better equipped to manage.
Custody.usage: Custody was the whole story of the FTX collapse — customers did not lose a trade, they lost their counterparty.

AMM.long:
An automated market maker replaces the order book with a pool of two assets and a formula. Traders swap against the pool, and the formula — most simply, keeping the product of the two balances constant — sets the price, which slides along a curve as the pool's balances shift.

Prices on an AMM come from nobody's opinion. They come from arbitrageurs trading the pool back into line with prices elsewhere. Liquidity providers deposit both assets and earn fees for standing on the other side of every trade, including the informed ones. That last clause is the catch, and it has a name: impermanent loss.

Where people get fooled: the fee yield is visible on a dashboard and the cost is not. Providing liquidity means systematically buying the asset that is falling and selling the one that is rising — being everyone's counterparty by construction. Whether the fees compensate for that depends on volume and volatility, not on the advertised rate, and often they do not.
AMM.usage: The pool quoted a noticeably worse price than the centralised venue for the same size, because an AMM curve rather than a market maker was setting the rate.

Impermanent loss.long:
Impermanent loss is what a liquidity provider gives up relative to simply holding the two deposited assets. When the price ratio moves, the AMM formula rebalances the pool against the provider: it sheds the appreciating asset and accumulates the depreciating one, so the position ends up worth less than an untouched fifty-fifty holding.

The word 'impermanent' is marketing. The loss only reverses if the price ratio returns to where you deposited; if it never does, the loss is entirely permanent and gets realised on withdrawal. The larger the divergence, the larger the gap. Fee income is supposed to compensate — sometimes it does, often it does not.

Where people get fooled: dashboards show fee income in bright green and divergence loss nowhere at all. Providers watch a healthy-looking yield while the position quietly underperforms a wallet that did nothing. The honest comparison is always against holding: if the pool position is worth less than the idle coins would have been, the yield was an illusion.
Impermanent loss.usage: The pair paid handsome fees all year, but one token tripled — impermanent loss meant simply holding both coins would have finished ahead.

Yield farming.long:
Yield farming is moving capital between DeFi protocols to harvest whatever they are paying — trading fees, lending interest, and above all token emissions. The headline rates that draw people in usually come from a protocol printing its own token and handing it out to depositors.

The mechanism matters: yield paid in a token the protocol invented is funded by dilution, and everyone farming it is selling it. Advertised rates therefore compress quickly, and the reward token's price often falls faster than the rewards accrue. Durable yield has an identifiable payer — a borrower paying interest, a trader paying fees — and is usually modest.

Where people get fooled: the APY figure gets read like interest on a bank deposit. It is a snapshot of an emissions schedule, denominated in a falling asset, quoted before smart-contract risk, impermanent loss and gas. The load-bearing question is who is paying the yield and why. If the answer is 'new depositors', the structure is a familiar one wearing a new interface.
Yield farming.usage: The farm's advertised rate collapsed within a fortnight as emissions were harvested and sold, revealing how little fee income sat underneath it.

Gas.long:
Gas is the fee paid to have a transaction included in a block. It is an auction: block space is scarce, users bid for it, and validators prioritise the highest bidders. Fees therefore spike exactly when everyone wants in or out at once — which is exactly when you most need to transact.

For a trader, gas is a cost-model item with nasty timing properties. It is charged per transaction rather than in proportion to size, so it quietly makes small positions uneconomic. And because congestion correlates with volatility, the cost of acting is highest during precisely the moves that matter.

Where people get fooled: backtests of on-chain strategies assume an average gas cost. But a strategy's busiest moments coincide with the network's busiest moments, so realised costs cluster at the worst prices rather than the mean. A system that looks profitable at average fees can be a steady loser once fees are sampled from the moments it actually trades.
Gas.usage: The arbitrage window existed for perhaps thirty seconds, but gas spiked with the volatility and consumed the entire margin on the trade.

MEV.long:
MEV — maximal extractable value — is profit extracted by whoever controls the ordering of transactions within a block. Because pending transactions are publicly visible before they confirm, searchers can insert their own trades ahead of, behind, or around yours: front-running, back-running, and the sandwich, which does both to a single swap.

The mechanism is structural, not a bug awaiting a patch. Your DEX trade broadcasts intent; bots bid gas to be sequenced around it; your fill worsens by roughly the amount extracted. Slippage tolerance settings are the crude defence, and a wide tolerance is an open invitation.

Where people get fooled: traders blame slippage or bad luck for persistently poor on-chain fills, as though the damage were random noise. Much of it is adversarial and systematic — a tax collected by better-positioned participants who saw the order first. On-chain execution is a game in which some players get to read your cards before deciding their move, and pricing that in is part of the cost model.
MEV.usage: The swap filled at the worst-case tolerance while the pool barely moved afterwards, which is the classic signature of being sandwiched.

Stablecoin.long:
A stablecoin is a token engineered to hold a fixed value, usually one US dollar. The mechanism behind the peg varies enormously: some are backed by dollars and Treasuries at a custodian, some by overcollateralised crypto, and some — historically the disasters — by algorithms and circular incentives with no hard assets at all.

Stablecoins are the plumbing of crypto trading: the quote currency for most pairs, the collateral behind most perps, the parking spot between trades. That makes their solvency everyone's problem. A stablecoin is only as sound as its reserves, its redemption mechanism and its issuer's honesty, and those three things differ wildly across issuers.

Where people get fooled: a price reading of one dollar gets mistaken for safety. The peg shows that arbitrage is functioning today, not that reserves exist. Holding a stablecoin is an uncollateralised loan to the issuer, and any yield on it is compensation for a risk most holders have decided not to examine. What backs it matters more than what the ticker shows.
Stablecoin.usage: Sitting out the week in stablecoins simply relocated the risk — from the market's volatility to the issuer's balance sheet.

Depeg.long:
A depeg is a stablecoin or other pegged asset trading away from its intended value. Small wobbles are routine and get closed by arbitrage. A genuine depeg begins when the arbitrage loop breaks — redemptions halt, reserves come into doubt — and holders race to be first through the exit.

The mechanics resemble a bank run. Confidence is the collateral of last resort: once enough holders sell below par, the discount itself becomes evidence that something is wrong, and the spiral feeds on its own output. Algorithmic designs have collapsed to nothing this way; asset-backed coins have survived deep discounts when redemption stayed open, because the arbitrage could still function.

Where people get fooled: a depegging coin looks like free money — a dollar on sale for ninety cents. That trade is a short position on the issuer's solvency: a small gain most of the time, a total loss occasionally. Sophisticated funds have bought historic depegs all the way to zero. Cheapness is not evidence of a floor.
Depeg.usage: During the depeg the pool drained one-sided, with everyone swapping out of the wounded coin at whatever price the curve offered.

On-chain metrics.long:
On-chain metrics are statistics read directly from a public blockchain: active addresses, transfer volumes, exchange inflows, the age of coins being moved. The pitch is that crypto offers what equities never did — a complete public ledger of activity, open to anyone with a query.

The catch is interpretation. Addresses are not people: one user can control thousands, and exchanges commingle millions. Exchange inflow gets read as selling intent, but transfers have many motives. And because the ledger is public and permissionless, the metrics are cheap to pollute — wash activity, spam transactions and incentivised address farming all leak into the data.

Where people get fooled: precision gets mistaken for meaning. A chart of inflows to eight decimal places still needs a behavioural story before it becomes a signal, and the stories are usually fitted after the move. The honest posture is to treat on-chain data as alternative data with severe labelling problems — occasionally informative, never the window into intent that the dashboards imply.
On-chain metrics.usage: Exchange inflows spiked before the drop, but the same metric also spiked before three rallies last quarter — the story reads far cleaner in hindsight.

Halving.long:
The halving is Bitcoin's scheduled supply event: roughly every four years, the block reward paid to miners is cut in half. It is written into the protocol, known decades in advance, and steadily reduces new issuance towards the cap of twenty-one million coins.

The bull case is simple supply and demand: less new supply against the same demand. The sceptical reply is just as simple: an event everyone has known about since 2009 should already be priced in, and the flow of new coins is now small next to daily trading volume. Past halvings sat near bull markets — alongside global liquidity cycles and much else that was moving at the same time.

Where people get fooled: with three or four observations, the 'halving cycle' is a sample-size illusion dressed up as a law of nature. Narratives fitted to a handful of data points feel rigorous because the dates are precise. The event is real and mechanical; the price prophecy built on top of it remains storytelling until there are many more cycles to count.
Halving.usage: He dates his entire market outlook off the halving cycle — a pattern with three whole observations behind it.

Wash trading.long:
Wash trading is trading with yourself — one entity on both sides of the same trade — to fabricate volume. No risk is transferred and no genuine price discovery occurs; the tape simply records activity that never economically happened.

In crypto the incentives are everywhere: exchanges wash to climb volume rankings, token teams wash to look liquid and win listings, NFT traders wash to farm reward tokens or fake a price floor. On unregulated venues there is no auditor and often no rule against it, and studies of exchange-reported volume have repeatedly found large fractions inconsistent with genuine activity.

Where people get fooled: volume is treated as the one honest statistic — price can lie, but volume confirms. On venues where volume is free to manufacture, it confirms nothing. Liquidity judged from reported turnover evaporates the moment real size tries to exit. Depth you can actually hit, not volume somebody reports, is the number that carries information.
Wash trading.usage: The token printed enormous reported volume, yet a modest sell order moved it double digits — the signature of a wash-traded tape.

24/7 market.long:
Crypto never closes: no opening auction, no weekend, no holidays. Positions carry around the clock, and anything — a hack, a headline, a cascade — can land at four on a Sunday morning against whatever leverage is sitting unattended.

This changes the risk mechanics, not just the schedule. There is no overnight gap in the equity sense, because price is always printing — but there are thin weekend books where modest size moves price violently. And there is no natural stopping point: no close to force a review, no bell that ends the session and sends everyone home.

Where people get fooled: continuous markets invite continuous involvement. People who would never day-trade equities end up checking charts at midnight, sleep-deprived, drip-feeding decisions at their personal worst. An always-open market gets read as opportunity; mechanically it mostly means the risk is always on, and discipline gets no closing bell to lean against. The market's schedule becomes the trader's schedule, which suits the market considerably more than the trader.
24/7 market.usage: The move landed at three in the morning local time — in a 24/7 market the risk stays awake regardless of who is asleep.

Layer 1 / Layer 2.long:
A Layer 1 is a base blockchain — Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana — that handles its own security and settlement. A Layer 2 is built on top: it processes transactions cheaply off the main chain and periodically settles back to it, inheriting the base layer's security with caveats attached.

The design exists because of a real constraint: a decentralised chain can only process so much, so block space gets expensive exactly when demand rises. Layer 2s trade extra trust assumptions — sequencers, bridges, exit mechanisms — for throughput and low fees. The caveats are where the risk lives.

Where people get fooled: 'inherits the base chain's security' gets heard as 'is the base chain'. Funds on a Layer 2 depend on bridge contracts, frequently a single sequencer, and exit procedures most users have never tested. For traders, the sharper exposure is narrative: 'the next big Layer 1' has been one of crypto's most frequently manufactured stories — a token category built for speculative rotation rather than for use.
Layer 1 / Layer 2.usage: Fees on the Layer 2 were pennies, but moving funds back to the main chain meant trusting the bridge and waiting out the exit window.

Bridge.long:
A bridge moves value between blockchains. Since chains cannot read each other, the usual mechanism is lock-and-mint: coins are locked in a contract or with a custodian on one chain, and a wrapped IOU is minted on the other. The IOU is only as good as the locked collateral and the code guarding it.

That locked pot makes bridges the honeypots of crypto — enormous value sitting behind a single contract or a small set of keys. Bridges have been one of the sector's major exploit vectors: several of the largest hacks in crypto's history drained bridge collateral and left the wrapped tokens on the far side unbacked.

Where people get fooled: a wrapped token gets treated as the asset itself. Wrapped bitcoin on another chain is not bitcoin; it is a claim on a bridge, carrying that bridge's custody and code risk, and it trades as if that risk were nil — right up until an exploit reprices it in an afternoon.
Bridge.usage: After the exploit the wrapped version traded at a discount to the native coin, because the collateral that backed it was gone.

Staking.long:
Staking is locking a proof-of-stake network's token to help validate transactions, in exchange for newly issued tokens and a share of fees. The stake is collateral: validators who cheat or go offline can be penalised — slashed — which is what secures the network in place of miners.

The advertised yield needs decomposing. Much of it is new issuance, which dilutes every holder — stakers are partly just reclaiming their own share — so the real return is the yield minus dilution, minus slashing risk, minus the lock-up. Unstaking often takes days or weeks, and the queue lengthens exactly when everyone wants out at once.

Where people get fooled: staking gets marketed as crypto's savings account. A savings account does not have a redemption queue that grows during a crash, a penalty regime for your validator's mistakes, or a principal that routinely moves double digits in a week. The yield is real, but it is small next to the volatility of the thing being staked, and the lock-up binds precisely when it hurts.
Staking.usage: The staking yield looked attractive until the unbonding period was read closely — weeks of forced holding through whatever the market does in between.

Liquid staking.long:
Liquid staking wraps ordinary staking in a tradeable receipt: deposit the token, receive a derivative token that accrues the staking yield and can be traded, lent or posted as collateral while the underlying stays locked with validators.

The receipt trades at a market price, not a promised peg. In calm conditions arbitrage holds it near the underlying; in stress it can slip to a meaningful discount, because redemption is slow and everyone is trying to leave through a narrow door at once. On top sit the provider's smart-contract risk and, in some designs, an uncomfortable concentration of the network's stake with one operator.

Where people get fooled: 'liquid' gets heard as 'riskless liquidity'. The liquidity is only as deep as the secondary market on a bad day. Traders who borrowed against liquid staking tokens have been liquidated by the discount alone — collateral falling against the very asset it supposedly represented, while the underlying network worked exactly as designed.
Liquid staking.usage: The receipt token slipped to a discount during the panic, and leveraged holders were liquidated on that gap rather than on anything the network did.

Slashing.long:
Slashing is the penalty regime of proof-of-stake: a validator that signs conflicting blocks — or, in some designs, stays offline too long — has part of its staked collateral destroyed by the protocol. Delegators who staked through that validator typically share the loss.

The mechanism is the point: stake only secures a network if it can genuinely be taken away. Honest, competent operators are slashed rarely, and most events are operational rather than malicious — a misconfigured failover signing twice, a software bug, correlated downtime across machines. Which means a delegator's slashing risk is mostly a bet on somebody else's operational discipline.

Where people get fooled: delegators compare validators on advertised yield and commission, treating slashing as a footnote. But the yield differences are basis points and a slashing event is a chunk of principal. Choosing a validator is an operational due-diligence problem wearing an interest-rate costume, and almost nobody performs the diligence — the decision is made on a sorted yield column instead.
Slashing.usage: The validator's failover misfired and double-signed, and every delegator shared the penalty — an ops error converted directly into lost principal.

Tokenomics.long:
Tokenomics is a token's economic design: total supply, the issuance schedule, who was allocated what at which price, when locked portions unlock, and what the token actually entitles a holder to — fees, governance, or nothing beyond resale.

The supply side is where the mechanics bite. A token with a small circulating float and a large locked allocation can show a flattering price and market cap while insiders wait out their vesting cliffs. The fully diluted valuation says what the market is implicitly paying for all future supply; the unlock calendar says when that supply arrives and from whom.

Where people get fooled: buyers study the chart and skip the spreadsheet. The chart prices the float; the spreadsheet shows years of scheduled selling from allocations bought at a fraction of the current price. Supply schedules feel like trivia until it registers that the people who designed the schedule are the ones who get to sell into it — and that the design was not an accident.
Tokenomics.usage: The price held up until the tokenomics arrived on schedule — the first large unlock doubled the sellable supply within a week.

Vesting / unlock.long:
Vesting is the schedule on which insiders — team, investors, advisers — gain the right to sell their allocated tokens. An unlock is the date a tranche becomes sellable. Cliffs release a large block at once; linear vesting drips supply out over months or years.

The mechanism is straightforward: unlocked tokens held by early buyers with a cost basis near zero are latent sell pressure, and the schedule is public. Markets often move ahead of the date — holders hedge or front-run — so the effect gets smeared across weeks rather than landing punctually. What matters is the tranche's size relative to the circulating float and to daily volume.

Where people get fooled: in both directions. Some ignore the calendar entirely and are baffled by 'mystery' selling. Others treat unlocks as a mechanical short signal, forgetting that a public date tends to be priced before it arrives. The calendar is context about supply, not a timing machine, and it rewards reading over reacting.
Vesting / unlock.usage: A tranche equal to a third of the float unlocks next month — the chart shows nothing, but the vesting schedule has it in writing.

TVL.long:
Total value locked is DeFi's headline size metric: the market value of all assets deposited in a protocol's contracts. It gets used as a proxy for adoption and trust, on the theory that capital does not sit in a contract nobody believes in.

The metric is softer than it looks. TVL is denominated in volatile assets, so it rises and falls with prices while actual deposits sit unchanged. It can be rented — protocols paying their own token for deposits are buying TVL, not earning it — and the same capital can be counted more than once through recursive lending and restaking loops.

Where people get fooled: TVL gets read as revenue, or as safety. It is neither. It is a gross balance, mercenary and often levered, that leaves the moment the incentives stop. Fee income relative to TVL, and how quickly the total drains when emissions taper, say far more about a protocol than the headline figure ever does — which is precisely why the headline figure is the one that gets marketed.
TVL.usage: The protocol's TVL halved without a single withdrawal, because the total was denominated in a token that halved first.

Oracle.long:
An oracle feeds off-chain information — mostly prices — onto the chain so that smart contracts can act on it. Lending protocols, perps and stablecoins all trigger liquidations and settlements from oracle prices, not from the price on any screen you happen to be watching.

That makes the oracle a load-bearing wall. If it lags, liquidations fire late or on stale prices. If it reads from a thin venue, an attacker can shove that one market briefly and trick the contract into mispricing collateral — oracle manipulation is one of DeFi's recurring exploit patterns, because moving a small market is cheaper than defrauding a large one directly.

Where people get fooled: users assume the protocol sees 'the market price', singular. It sees one constructed feed with particular sources, update intervals and failure modes. Positions have been liquidated off a wick that existed on a single venue for under a minute. The oracle design is fine print, and it is the fine print that decides where your liquidation actually happens.
Oracle.usage: The liquidation printed at the oracle's price, not the price on the trader's screen — the feed lagged the crash by most of a minute.

Open interest (crypto).long:
Open interest is the total value of derivative contracts currently open — every long matched against a short. In crypto it is watched mainly on perpetuals, where it measures how much leveraged exposure exists right now, venue by venue.

Rising open interest means new positions opening; falling means positions closing or being liquidated. Read alongside price and funding, it sketches the positioning: price rising on rising OI suggests fresh longs, price rising on falling OI suggests shorts covering. High open interest is fuel — the more leverage stacked at similar entries, the more violent the cascade when price reaches the crowd's liquidation zone.

Where people get fooled: open interest narratives get promoted into directional signals with an authority the data cannot carry. The same OI print supports opposite stories, and the labels — trapped shorts, smart-money accumulation — are mostly applied after the move has resolved. Open interest tells you how much leverage exists and roughly where; it does not tell you which way the resolution runs.
Open interest (crypto).usage: Open interest climbed all week while price went sideways — a growing stack of leverage waiting to be resolved in one direction or the other.

Basis / cash-and-carry.long:
Basis is the gap between a derivative's price and spot. The recurring crypto version: futures and perps trading above spot because leveraged longs outnumber shorts. Cash-and-carry harvests the gap — buy spot, short the derivative against it, and collect the difference as prices converge or as funding accrues to the short leg.

The position is neutral on price but on nothing else. The return comes from a basis that compresses exactly when too much capital chases it, and the risks sit at the edges: counterparty exposure on the venue holding the short leg, margin calls if the basis widens before it narrows, and fee drag on two legs instead of one.

Where people get fooled: 'market-neutral' gets heard as 'risk-free'. The steady drip of small basis gains conceals a short position in tail events — venue insolvency, a collateral depeg, a funding regime flip. The 2022 exchange failures turned a number of tidy carry books into unsecured bankruptcy claims, which is the tail showing up on schedule.
Basis / cash-and-carry.usage: With the perp trading rich to spot, the desk ran cash-and-carry — long the coin, short the perp, clipping the basis while it lasted.

Proof of reserves.long:
Proof of reserves is an exchange publishing evidence that it holds customer assets — typically a Merkle-tree snapshot letting each user verify their balance was included, plus signed wallet addresses demonstrating the coins exist on-chain.

The mechanism proves assets, not solvency. A venue can display a billion in coins while owing two billion; reserves without liabilities are half a balance sheet. Snapshots can be dressed up with borrowed coins returned after the photograph, and obligations to lenders, hidden leverage and encumbered collateral appear on no chain at all.

Where people get fooled: the word 'proof' does the fooling. It suggests audit-grade assurance, when most schemes are unaudited snapshots with no liability side and no opinion from anyone independent. After the FTX collapse the phrase became a marketing checkbox within weeks. It is better than nothing and meaningfully weaker than a real audit — and it is no substitute for the one protection that requires no trust in anybody, which is withdrawing to self-custody.
Proof of reserves.usage: The proof of reserves showed the assets and said nothing about the liabilities — half a balance sheet, presented with the confidence of an audit.

Cold vs hot wallet.long:
A hot wallet's keys live on an internet-connected device — a browser extension, a phone, an exchange's operational wallet. A cold wallet's keys are generated and kept offline, on a hardware device or an air-gapped machine, signing transactions without ever exposing the key to the network.

The distinction is attack surface. Hot wallets are convenient and continuously exposed: malware, phishing, malicious token approvals, a compromised device. Cold storage removes the online attack path and substitutes physical and procedural risks — losing the device, botching the backup, or being talked into signing something malicious anyway.

Where people get fooled: the hardware device becomes a talisman. A cold wallet does not protect anyone from approving a malicious transaction on its own screen, from a seed phrase typed 'just once' into a website, or from a tampered device bought second-hand. The security model is the entire procedure around the keys — the gadget is one link in that chain, and rarely the weakest one. The weakest link is usually the person holding it.
Cold vs hot wallet.usage: The trading float lives in a hot wallet for convenience; everything else sits cold, where a phished browser session cannot reach it.

Seed phrase.long:
A seed phrase is the human-readable master key to a wallet — usually twelve or twenty-four words that deterministically generate every private key inside it. Whoever holds the words holds the funds: no password, no second factor, no undo.

This yields the simplest security rule in crypto: every request for your seed phrase is theft. No exchange, wallet developer, support agent or 'validation service' ever needs it. The entire scam industry around crypto — fake support desks, fake airdrops, fake wallet updates — is machinery for making that one request sound legitimate for one moment.

Where people get fooled: not by exotic attacks but by plausible context. The request arrives moments after a real problem, inside a convincing interface, with urgency attached — verify now or lose access. People who know the rule perfectly well in calm moments type the words in panicked ones. The rule's strength is that it admits no exceptions, which is exactly what makes it usable under stress: there is nothing to weigh up.
Seed phrase.usage: The 'support agent' asked him to verify his seed phrase — which was the entire scam, since every such request is theft.

Airdrop.long:
An airdrop is a free distribution of tokens, usually to wallets that used a protocol early. The commercial logic is marketing: seed a user base, decentralise ownership on paper, and conjure a market price for a token that otherwise has no natural buyers.

The mechanism attracts industrial gaming. Airdrop farmers run thousands of wallets performing minimal qualifying actions, so much of the apparent activity before a rumoured drop is mercenary rather than organic. On distribution day the recipients' cost basis is zero, and the rational farmer sells immediately — which is why so many airdropped tokens chart as a cliff with a long tail.

Where people get fooled: twice over. Recipients treat the tokens as a windfall to hold, anchored to an opening print that the sell-off promptly makes irrelevant. Observers read pre-airdrop activity metrics as growth when they largely measure bot farms. Free tokens are real money — but the freeness sits on the sell side too, and the sellers move first.
Airdrop.usage: The protocol's activity halved the week after the airdrop, once the farmers had collected their tokens and moved on.

Memecoin.long:
A memecoin is a token whose stated value proposition is the joke itself — no cash flows, no utility claims, just attention. The candour is almost refreshing: it is a pure bet on other people buying later, and unlike most of crypto it says so out loud.

The market mechanics are brutal and fast. Insiders and bots hold large, cheap positions from the first minutes; liquidity is thin and frequently removable; the lifecycle — launch, viral spike, exhaustion, bleed — plays out in days. A few legacy names persist as tradeable attention indices, while thousands of others round-trip to zero, with the rug pull as the explicit exit-scam variant.

Where people get fooled: by the visible winners. Every cycle produces a handful of spectacular multiplication stories that recruit the next cohort, who arrive as exit liquidity for the wallets that were present first. Survivorship does the selling — the graveyard of identical tokens that went nowhere is invisible, and the graveyard is very nearly the whole population.
Memecoin.usage: It is a memecoin — the whitepaper is a dog picture, and every participant's plan is to sell to somebody who arrives later.

Exchange outage.long:
An exchange outage is the venue going down — the matching engine stalls, the API returns errors, the app shows a spinner — while the market elsewhere keeps moving. In crypto, outages cluster at the worst possible times, because record volatility and record load are the same event.

The mechanics punish leveraged traders hardest: you cannot close, add margin or cancel orders, while the liquidation engine, running inside the venue's own systems, frequently keeps working. Positions have been liquidated while their owners stared at error pages. Outages during cascades also amplify them, because resting liquidity vanishes exactly as the forced flow arrives.

Where people get fooled: outage risk is priced at zero until the day it prices itself. Traders size positions as though the exit door is always open, when the history of nearly every major venue says otherwise. The honest planning assumption is that access fails during precisely the move that matters — which is the moment a plan that depends on clicking buttons stops being a plan.
Exchange outage.usage: The app was down for forty minutes during the flush — orders would not cancel, but the liquidations went through without any trouble.

Insurance fund.long:
An insurance fund is a derivatives exchange's buffer against bankrupt positions. When a trader is liquidated beyond their margin — price gapped through the liquidation level before the engine could act — the fund absorbs the shortfall so that winning traders are still paid in full.

The fund is filled from liquidation residue: positions closed slightly better than their bankruptcy price leave a remainder the venue keeps. It therefore grows in choppy, liquidation-rich conditions and drains in one-way crashes — which is exactly when it is needed most. If it runs dry, the venue falls back on socialised losses or auto-deleveraging, clawing the shortfall back from profitable accounts.

Where people get fooled: the fund's headline size gets read as a guarantee. It is a buffer of unstated adequacy, controlled by the venue, governed by rules the venue can rewrite. What it actually covers is discovered during the event itself — which is also when traders learn, by demonstration, what auto-deleveraging means for a winning position.
Insurance fund.usage: Price gapped clean through the bankruptcy level, and the insurance fund absorbed the difference so the winning side was paid out in full.

Auto-deleveraging.long:
Auto-deleveraging — ADL — is the last resort in a perp exchange's loss waterfall. When liquidations cannot be absorbed by the market and the insurance fund is exhausted, the venue force-closes traders on the winning side, typically the most profitable and most leveraged first, at the bankruptcy price of the failed positions.

The mechanism exists because a derivatives venue is a closed system: every dollar won must be paid by a loser. If the losing side's margin and the fund together cannot cover the bill, the money simply does not exist — so the venue cancels part of the winning side instead. On some venues ADL has closed profitable positions mid-crash, capping exactly the trades that were working.

Where people get fooled: traders assume a winning position with sensible risk management is safe from the venue's problems. Under ADL a profitable short can be taken away at the worst moment, not through any error of yours, but because the opposite side of the ledger went bankrupt. It is counterparty risk wearing an engine-room name.
Auto-deleveraging.usage: The short was auto-deleveraged during the crash — closed at the bankruptcy price while the move was still running in its favour.

Isolated vs cross margin.long:
Margin mode decides what a losing position can take down with it. Isolated margin walls each position off with its own allocated collateral: lose it, and the damage stops there. Cross margin pools the whole account behind every position: more room before liquidation, because everything you hold is the buffer.

The trade-off is mechanical. Isolated gives a known worst case per trade but liquidates earlier, since only the allocated margin defends the position. Cross survives larger swings but converts one bad trade into a claim on the entire balance — and when several positions share collateral, a loser shifts the liquidation prices of everything else in the account.

Where people get fooled: the switch to cross usually happens mid-drawdown, to push a liquidation price further away rather than admit a position has failed. That converts a defined loss into a survival question — the margin-mode cousin of averaging down. The setting looks like plumbing; it is actually a maximum-loss policy, and it is far better chosen in advance than improvised under stress.
Isolated vs cross margin.usage: The position was on isolated margin, so the liquidation cost its allocated collateral and nothing else — on cross, the entire account would have stood behind it.

Perp funding arbitrage.long:
Perp funding arbitrage collects the funding rate while holding no net price exposure: short the perpetual, hold the same value in spot — or the reverse when funding runs negative — and receive the periodic payments the leveraged crowd is making for its positioning.

The return is a crowd-sentiment premium, not a free lunch. Funding is fattest when speculation runs hottest, and it compresses as arbitrage capital arrives to collect it. The costs live in the mechanics: fees and slippage on two legs, collateral parked on a venue that can fail, margin risk on the short leg during spikes, and long stretches where funding flips against the position.

Where people get fooled: by annualising the current funding print. A juicy rate at this instant, multiplied out to a yearly figure, assumes a regime that historically refuses to persist. In practice the strategy earns a modest, lumpy carry with genuine tail risk — the 2022 venue failures converted several neutral carry books into unsecured claims. It is a thin-margin business, not a yield button.
Perp funding arbitrage.usage: Funding stayed positive all month, so the desk sat short perps against spot, collecting the periodic payments from the leveraged long side.

Evaluation.long:
An evaluation is a prop firm's paid entry exam: trade a simulated account to a profit target under drawdown and consistency rules, and the firm labels the account 'funded'. Break a rule at any point and the fee is spent; another fee buys another attempt.

The business model deserves plain statement: evaluation fees are revenue whether or not anyone passes. Many firms earn primarily from failed attempts and resets rather than from the trading of those who get through — which means the rule set is calibrated as product design, tight enough to be difficult, loose enough to look passable from the outside.

Where people get fooled: the exam gets treated as a measure of skill. Fixed targets against tight loss caps reward fast, aggressive trading over the patient kind that survives in real markets, so passing often selects for luck plus aggression rather than for edge. The honest arithmetic is expected cost — fee times attempts, a sum each person can run for themselves — paid up front, against a payout that stays hypothetical until independently verified.
Evaluation.usage: He is on his fourth evaluation this quarter, and each attempt was a fresh fee regardless of what happened afterwards.

Profit target.long:
In prop-firm terms, the profit target is the fixed percentage gain on the simulated account that must be reached to pass an evaluation — inside a rule set that simultaneously caps losses per day and overall, and often expects the result within a limited stretch of trading days.

The structure creates a specific distortion. A fixed target sitting above a tighter loss cap pushes traders towards leverage and frequency: the geometry rewards a lucky streak of aggressive bets and punishes the slow grind of small edges. In other words, it selects for roughly the opposite of what durable trading looks like, which suits the seller of attempts perfectly well.

Where people get fooled: the target frames the account as nearly-earned money — just a few percent to go — which invites doubling risk when behind schedule. The firm's own rules make busting on that behaviour the likely outcome, and each bust sells another attempt. A target that changes how you trade is not a milestone; it is a working part of the product's failure machinery.
Profit target.usage: Two good days short of the profit target, he doubled his size to finish early — and met the daily loss limit instead.

Trailing drawdown.long:
A trailing drawdown is a loss limit that follows your equity peak upwards instead of staying anchored at the starting balance. Make money and the floor rises beneath you — and on many firms' accounts it trails the unrealised peak, the best moment of an open trade, not just banked profit.

The mechanics are harsher than the marketing copy admits. Let a winner run to a new high-water mark and the floor climbs with it: open profit becomes a raised floor, and a routine pullback in a still-valid trade can end the account. The rule converts ordinary trade management — giving positions room to work — into a violation.

Where people get fooled: traders read 'maximum drawdown' and picture the static number from their backtests. Trailing-from-unrealised-peak is a different object entirely: it taxes exactly the behaviour, holding winners, that most strategies depend on, and accounts die under it while net profitable. Understanding precisely how the floor moves, before any money changes hands, is most of the game.
Trailing drawdown.usage: The trade ran up nicely, pulled back to breakeven, and the account failed — the trailing drawdown had converted the open-profit peak into the new floor.

Intraday vs end-of-day drawdown.long:
The distinction is when the loss limit is measured. An end-of-day drawdown checks equity once, at the session close; an intraday version watches continuously, so any moment's dip — including open-trade fluctuation — can breach it. Two accounts advertising the same limit can behave completely differently.

Mechanically, intraday measurement taxes volatility rather than losses. A position that dips against you before working — routine in any strategy with normal noise — can end an intraday-measured account even when the day finishes green. End-of-day measurement forgives the path and judges the outcome, which is much closer to how backtest drawdown is actually computed.

Where people get fooled: traders port position sizes from backtests that measured drawdown on daily closes into accounts that measure it tick by tick. The same strategy at the same size then fails the intraday rule on path noise the backtest never registered. The two regimes demand different sizing, and firms rarely advertise in large print which one they run.
Intraday vs end-of-day drawdown.usage: The day closed in profit, but the account had already failed at lunchtime — the drawdown was measured intraday, not at the close.

Consistency rule.long:
A consistency rule caps how much of total profit may come from a single day or trade — exceed the permitted fraction and the pass or payout is withheld until the distribution evens out. Firms present it as filtering gamblers from professionals.

The mechanical effect is different: it selects against lumpy but genuine strategies. Plenty of real edges earn their year in a handful of outsized days — trend-following and news-driven approaches especially — and a consistency rule makes exactly that profile a violation. What it favours instead is steady small-scale grinding, which the firm's other rules and costs are well placed to erode.

Where people get fooled: the rule sounds like prudent risk management, so it gets accepted uninspected. In practice it operates as a payout gate — profitable accounts denied or delayed for distribution reasons unrelated to risk — and it nudges traders into padding quiet days with unnecessary trades purely to rebalance the ledger. Manufactured activity to satisfy a metric is not risk control; it is the opposite.
Consistency rule.usage: One strong trend day made up most of the month's profit, so the consistency rule held the payout back until more trading days diluted it.

Payout split.long:
The payout split is the advertised division of simulated profits between trader and firm, with the trader keeping the headline share. The split applies only to profits the firm's rules allow out of the door — which is where the attention belongs.

The machinery around the split matters more than the split. Minimum trading days, consistency conditions, payout caps and review windows all sit between a green account and money arriving. And since most accounts are simulated, the firm pays winners out of company revenue — largely other traders' fees — which makes payout policy a cash-flow decision for the firm rather than a share of real trading gains.

Where people get fooled: the generous headline number is the marketing; the denial conditions are the product. A large split on profits that rarely survive the rule gauntlet is worth less than a modest split paid promptly and verifiably. The split answers 'how much'; the questions that decide whether anything arrives are 'when' and 'whether', and they live in the fine print.
Payout split.usage: The split sounded generous, but the conditions between profit and payment — minimum days, consistency check, review window — decided what actually arrived.

Reset fee.long:
A reset fee buys a fresh start on a failed or damaged evaluation — the account returns to its starting balance and rules, priced below the original evaluation fee. It is presented as a courtesy. It functions as the firm's most efficient product.

The economics are stark: the marginal cost of resetting a simulated account is nil, so resets are nearly pure margin, sold at the precise moment the customer is most motivated to buy — immediately after a near miss. Discount campaigns and flash reset sales cluster accordingly. Fees are revenue whether or not anyone passes, and resets are that revenue on repeat.

Where people get fooled: each reset gets justified as 'nearly passed last time'. Run the arithmetic yourself — fee times the attempts you realistically expect — and the true price of a funded account comes out at several multiples of the sticker. The reset converts a one-off exam fee into a subscription, with the sunk-cost fallacy quietly handling customer retention.
Reset fee.usage: Three resets in, he had spent more than double the original evaluation fee — 'nearly passed' turned out to be the expensive place to live.

Scaling plan.long:
A scaling plan is a firm's schedule for growing a funded account: hit milestones — profit levels, time survived, clean rule compliance — and the notional balance or permitted size steps up, with the implied promise of large capital at the top of the ladder.

The mechanism worth examining is where failure risk sits during the climb. Every rung is a fresh exam: larger size against the same trailing drawdown and daily limits, where one violation typically drops or ends the account. The impressive figures at the top are conditional on surviving every step under rules that make survival the difficult part.

Where people get fooled: the top rung gets read as the offer. Marketing displays the six-figure end state; the binding constraint is failure risk compounded across every step on the way there. Few paths survive the whole ladder, and the firm's economics rather depend on that. The plan itself is real — treating it as a destination rather than a gauntlet is the error.
Scaling plan.usage: The scaling plan doubles the account at each milestone, provided nothing in the rulebook is touched anywhere on the way up.

News trading restriction.long:
A news trading restriction forbids holding or opening positions around scheduled high-impact releases — central bank decisions, inflation prints, payrolls — typically within a defined window either side of the timestamp. Some firms void profits made inside the window; others fail the account outright.

The stated rationale is protection from slippage in thin, violent markets. The firm's deeper interest is more specific: news windows are where simulated fills diverge most from anything achievable in a live market, and where traders most easily bank fast simulated profits that the firm would have to pay out in real money. The rule protects the firm's cash flow first, and the trader's account second.

Where people get fooled: the restriction sits deep in the rulebook and gets enforced retroactively. A trader holds through a release without realising, profits, and the payout review discovers the violation weeks later. Accounts have been voided over positions held seconds inside a window. The releases are on a public calendar; the firm's exact window definition is the detail that decides everything.
News trading restriction.usage: The trade went on ninety seconds before the announcement — inside the firm's news window — so the profit was voided at payout review.

Simulated funding.long:
Simulated funding is the quiet fact underneath most of the modern prop industry: the 'funded account' is a demo. By default no trade touches a live market — a firm's risk desk may copy a small subset of traders into real venues, but the standard arrangement is that your fills, and your profits, exist inside the firm's software.

The economics follow directly. Payouts come from company revenue — evaluation fees, resets, subscriptions — rather than from trading gains, so the structure resembles an insurance book: many small premiums collected, the occasional winner paid, solvency resting on fees exceeding payouts. Every rule that reduces payouts is therefore load-bearing.

Where people get fooled: 'funded' gets heard as 'trading the firm's capital'. Almost nothing in the arrangement requires real capital to exist, and payout reliability rests on the firm's fee income and goodwill rather than on any brokerage account. The model works while inflows are strong; the failure mode arrives when new-fee revenue slows and the queue of pending payouts does not.
Simulated funding.usage: The account was simulated end to end, so the payout, when it came, was paid from the firm's revenue rather than from any market.

Copy trading a funded account.long:
This is running the same trades across several funded or evaluation accounts at once — your own, or by copying a 'master' account onto customers' logins as a passing service. Firms ban most versions of it, third-party copying and group passing services especially.

The mechanics explain both the appeal and the ban. When accounts are simulated, copying costs nothing to replicate, so one lucky streak becomes many simultaneous payout claims — a direct raid on the firm's fee pool. Firms answer with detection: matching trade timestamps, sizes and network fingerprints across accounts, then voiding payouts at review, often after months of apparent success.

Where people get fooled: sellers of passing and copying services collect their fee up front, while the buyer carries all of the ban risk. Detection tends to land exactly when a payout is requested, because that is when firms look hardest — and every linked account can be voided together. The scheme's profits are contingent right up until paid; the service fee, naturally, was real money from the start.
Copy trading a funded account.usage: One strategy was copied across five accounts; the review matched the timestamps and voided all five payouts in a single decision.

Consistent profitability.long:
Consistent profitability is the industry's phrase for the actual goal: an edge that survives costs, regime changes and enough trades to distinguish it from luck. It is a property of a large sample, not of a good month — which is precisely what makes it hard to verify, in yourself or in anyone selling you something.

Mechanically, consistency means expectancy holding up across time and conditions, with drawdowns that capital and temperament can carry. A genuine edge still produces losing weeks and flat quarters as ordinary variance; a coin-flipper still produces impressive months. Short windows cannot tell the two apart, which is why sample size sits underneath every honest claim.

Where people get fooled: the phrase gets defined backwards — a smooth recent stretch is labelled 'consistent' and extrapolated forwards. Sellers lean on this reflex: a screenshot of one good run is the industry's core marketing asset. Anybody's smooth stretch, your own included, is weak evidence until the trade count is large and the period spans more than one market mood.
Consistent profitability.usage: Six green weeks is not consistent profitability yet — it is a short sample that has not met a bad regime.

Evaluation expected cost.long:
The expected cost of a funded account is not the sticker fee. It is the fee multiplied by the number of attempts a realistic trader needs, plus resets and subscriptions along the way. That multiplication is the honest price tag, and every reader can run it with their own assumptions.

The mechanism hiding the cost is per-attempt framing. Each fee looks small and each failure looks like an anomaly — nearly passed — so attempts accumulate without ever being added up. The rules themselves, trailing drawdowns and daily limits and consistency conditions, are what set the attempt count high; the firm's revenue is exactly your attempt count times the fee.

Where people get fooled: by comparing the sticker fee against an imagined funded payout, rather than comparing the summed spend against payouts that can actually be verified. Framed honestly, an evaluation is a repeated purchase of a long-odds ticket where the seller sets the terms and can revise them. That may still be worth buying for some people — but only at its true, multiplied price, decided in advance.
Evaluation expected cost.usage: Before the first attempt she wrote down the arithmetic — fee times a realistic number of tries — and treated that figure as the actual price.

Payout verification.long:
Payout verification is checking that a prop firm actually pays — not that it promises to, but that money reliably leaves the firm and lands with traders, at the advertised split, within the advertised time. It is the only metric that finally matters, and the hardest to observe from outside.

The evidence environment is poor. Firms publish self-reported, unaudited 'total paid out' figures; testimonial screenshots are trivially faked and frequently incentivised through affiliate programmes; denials happen quietly, case by case, inside rule reviews. The visible record is therefore systematically rosier than the underlying reality. Payment processors dropping a firm, or payout terms changing abruptly, carry more information than anything on the firm's own site.

Where people get fooled: verification gets attempted through the firm's own channels — its community server, its published totals, its affiliated reviewers — all selected or paid by the subject of the inquiry. The workable standard is independent, dated, repeated evidence from traders with no referral link. Almost nothing in the industry's marketing meets it, which is itself informative.
Payout verification.usage: The firm's payout wall was screenshots from affiliates top to bottom — nothing on it qualified as independent payout verification.

Two-step vs one-step.long:
This is the structure of the evaluation gauntlet. A one-step account has a single profit target to pass; a two-step adds a second phase, usually with a lower target under the same rules, before the 'funded' label. Two-step fees are typically lower per attempt; the path is longer.

The comparison is a pricing exercise, not a preference. Each extra phase multiplies the opportunities to fail, since a rule violation ends the run at any stage — so a cheaper fee on a longer gauntlet can easily cost more per funded account than a dearer single step. The figure that matters is total expected spend to reach a verified payout: fee times realistic attempts across all phases, not the sticker on either product.

Where people get fooled: the choice is marketed like a difficulty setting, as though the firm were indifferent. It is pricing design — fee, target and rules are calibrated on both routes so the firm's revenue per funded account works either way. The drawdown definition often differs between the two products at the same firm, and that detail decides more outcomes than the step count does.
Two-step vs one-step.usage: He chose the one-step for the shorter path, then noticed its trailing drawdown was stricter than the two-step's — the products differed where it mattered.
